title: Speech rooted in the mind
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hookLine: a boy tells his teacher an awkward truth, and a chant asks words and mind to match
carry: satya: let your words match your mind
tomorrow: what's hidden behind a lid made of gold?

lines: THE PLAIN TRUTH, WORD FOR WORD.
YOU HAVEN'T STRAYED FROM THE TRUTH.
cards: A boy named Satyakama wants to study the Veda, and a teacher will ask about his family line. So he asks his mother.

She tells him the plain truth: she was young, working as a servant in many houses, and she doesn't know his line. Just say you're Satyakama, son of Jabala. So he does, word for word, to the teacher Gautama.
And Gautama says: no one but a true brahmin could speak like that. You haven't strayed from the truth. Go fetch firewood.

teach.b: That story is in the Chandogya, and it sits close to today's chant, the one tradition sets with the Aitareya Upanishad, known by its first words, van me manasi.
In plain words: may my speech be rooted in my mind, and my mind rooted in my speech. May what I have heard not leave me. I will speak what is right.
I will speak what is true. May that protect me, and protect the one who speaks. Om, peace, peace, peace.
This is satya, truthfulness, one of the oldest pillars of dharma: Patanjali lists it among the first restraints of yoga, right after not harming. And the chant gives it an exact shape.
Truth is words and mind standing in the same place. Satyakama's words cost him; they matched his mind anyway. The tradition also argues about the other half of the line.

teach.h: THE RECITERS: THE SOUND IS SACRED.
teach.b: The reciters keep every syllable of the Veda exactly, because the sound itself is held sacred.

teach.h: YASKA: A POST CARRYING A LOAD.
teach.b: Yaska, an early teacher of what Vedic words mean, compares someone who recites without understanding to a post carrying a load.

teach.h: WORDS AND MIND IN ONE PLACE.
teach.b: The chant holds both: exact words, rooted in the mind.

how: Van me manasi is chanted as the peace chant of the Aitareya Upanishad; in traditional Vedic schools students learn recitation by ear, syllable by syllable, while commentators teach what the words mean.

games.q: what does “then two weeks of the peace chants” mean?
o: a vow to stay silent during holy study
a prayer asking for a good singing voice
a chant: may my speech and mind be rooted together

games.q: the chant and the argument. tap the pairs.
p: the plain truth, word for word
keep every syllable; the sound is sacred

s: Gautama turned Satyakama away because his family line was unknown
he took him in: only a true brahmin, he said, could speak such truth.
everyone in the tradition agrees that reciting without meaning is pointless
reciters hold the exact sound sacred; Yaska's post-and-load picture is the other side, and the chant asks for both.
Patanjali lists satya, truthfulness, among the restraints of yoga

games.q: you think understanding matters most. a friend who chants daily without knowing Sanskrit asks if she's wasting her time. give the reciters' best case.
o: yes, she is, until she learns the language properly.
the sound itself is held sacred; said exactly, it's already an offering.
meaning never matters in any Hindu practice, so she's fine.
games.why: the reciters' side: exact sound is sacred and keeps the text alive. Yaska's side asks for meaning. the chant itself wants both.

practice: The chant makes a promise: satyam vadishyami, I will speak what is true. If you pray, say those words softly, once or three times, the way the chant is said. If you don't, say it in English: I will speak what is true.

Then choose one true sentence about today, short and plain, and say it out loud, slowly, meaning each word as it leaves you. Let the rest of the sit be quiet, words and mind standing in the same place.

wordCard.voice: The peace chants, and today van me manasi: may my speech be rooted in my mind, and my mind in my speech.

orig.note: Sanskrit: my speech, in my mind; the first words of the Aitareya's peace chant.

carryVoice: Something to keep: satya, let your words match your mind. Satyakama's did. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: the peace chant van me manasi pratishthita (… ritam vadishyami, satyam vadishyami, tan mam avatu, tad vaktaram avatu …), chanted with the Aitareya Upanishad
